8            F.  Homesite’s Duty to Defend                                   
9       On July 29, 2022, Homesite sent a letter to Ms. Schlackman informing her that Homesite 
10  would agree to defend her in the Underlying Action subject to a full reservation of Homesite’s 
11  coverage rights. Dkt. # 12-4. On August 8, 2022, Homesite filed the instant action, seeking 
12  declaratory judgment from this Court that it was not obligated to defend or indemnify Ms. 
13  Schlackman in the Underlying Action. Dkt. # 1. On February 2, 2023, Homesite filed the instant 
14  motion for summary judgment. Dkt. # 11. Neither Ms. Schlackman nor the other defendants in 
15  this lawsuit (claimants in the Underlying Action) have answered Homesite’s complaint or 
16  responded to the motion for summary judgment.                            
17      II.  Legal Standard                                                  
18      A party is entitled to summary judgment if the “movant shows that there is no genuine 
19  dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Fed. 
20  R. Civ. P. 56(a). Under Rule 56, the party seeking summary dismissal of the case “bears the 
21  initial responsibility of informing the district court of the basis for its motion,” Celotex Corp. v. 
22  Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 323 (1986), and “citing to particular parts of materials in the record” that 
23  establish the absence of a genuine issue of material fact, Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c). Once the moving 
24  party satisfies its burden, it is entitled to summary judgment if the non-moving party fails to 
25  designate “specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial.” Celotex, 477 U.S. at 324 
26  (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(e)). The Court must “view the evidence in the light most favorable 
27  to the nonmovant and draw all reasonable inferences in the nonmovant’s favor.” City of Pomona 
28  v. SQM N. Am. Corp., 750 F.3d 1036, 1049 (9th Cir. 2014). Although the Court must reserve 
1  genuine issues regarding credibility, the weight of the evidence, and legitimate inferences for the 
2  trier of fact, the “mere existence of a scintilla of evidence in support of the non-moving party’s 
3  position will be insufficient” to avoid judgment. Id. (quoting Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 
4  477 U.S. 242, 252 (1986)). “Where the record taken as a whole could not lead a rational trier of 
5  fact to find for the nonmoving party, there is no genuine issue for trial.” Id. (quoting Matsushita 
6  Elec. Indus. Co., Ltd. v. Zenith Radio Corp., 475 U.S. 574, 587 (1986)).  
7       Even when a motion for summary judgment is unopposed, as here, the moving party 
8  retains its burden to demonstrate the absence of any issue of material fact. See Cristobal v. 
9  Siegel, 26 F.3d 1488, 1494-95 (9th Cir. 1994). District courts resolving unopposed summary 
10  judgment motions have an obligation to independently evaluate the sufficiency of the moving 
11  papers. Id. at 1496.                                                     
12      A. Timing of the Motion                                              
13      As an initial matter, the Court notes that plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment has 
14  been filed before defendants have filed their answers to the complaint and before the Court has 
15  issued a discovery order. Under Rule 56, “a party may file a motion for summary judgment at 
16  any time until 30 days after the close of all discovery.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(b) (emphasis added). 
17  Accordingly, “[c]ourts and commentators have acknowledged that no answer need be filed 
18  before a . . . motion for summary judgment may be entertained.” Marquez v. Cable One, Inc., 
19  463 F.3d 1118, 1120 (10th Cir. 2006) (quoting INVST Fin. Group, Inc. v. Chem-Nuclear Sys., 
20  Inc., 815 F.2d 391, 404 (6th Cir. 1987)).                                
21      However, even where a motion for summary judgment is technically compliant with the 
22  Rule, “in many cases [a] motion [filed at the commencement of an action] will be premature 
23  until the nonmovant has had time to file a responsive pleading or other pretrial proceedings have 
24  been had.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 56 advisory committee’s notes to 2010 amendment. Accordingly, 
25  district courts have sometimes denied pre-answer and pre-discovery motions for summary 
26  judgment as premature, particularly where discovery is needed to resolve factual disputes. See, 
27  e.g., Williams v. Yuan Chen, No. C10-1292CKD, 2011 WL 4354533, at *3 (E.D. Cal. Sept. 16, 
28  2011) (denying the plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment as premature where the defendant 
1  had not yet filed an answer and the court had not issued a discovery order); Waters v. Experian 
2  Info. Solutions, Inc., No. C12-308AJB-RBB, 2012 WL 1965333, at *4 n.2 (S.D. Cal. May 31, 
3  2012) (stating “[t]his Court typically finds pre-answer summary judgments premature and 
4  unhelpful”); Moore v. Hubbard, No. C06-2187FCD-EFB, 2009 WL 688897, at *1 (E.D. Cal. 
5  Mar. 13, 2009) (denying plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment as premature where 
6  “discovery has not yet begun, defendants have not yet filed an answer and the court has yet to 
7  issue a discovery and scheduling order”); Turner v. Cnty. of San Diego, No. C14-2003JAH-JLB, 
8  2016 WL 6804998, at * (S.D. Cal. Oct. 3, 2016) (same).                    
9       Here, the Court finds that although defendants have not yet answered plaintiff’s 
10  complaint, and no discovery order has been issued by the Court, plaintiff’s motion for summary 
11  judgment is not premature. Plaintiff asks the Court to enter a declaratory judgment “that it owes 
12  no duty to defend and/or indemnify Ms. Schlackman from the claims alleged in the Underlying 
13  Lawsuit.” Dkt. # 1 at 15. To determine whether an insurer has a duty to defend, courts look to 
14  “the ‘eight corners’ of the insurance contract and the underlying complaint.” Expedia, Inc. v. 
15  Steadfast Ins. Co., 180 Wn. 2d 793, 803 (2014). Thus, as plaintiff provides both the relevant 
16  insurance contract and underlying complaint with its motion, additional factual development 
17  through discovery is unnecessary to resolve the question raised in plaintiff’s motion for 
18  summary judgment.                                                        
19      III.  Discussion                                                     
20           A. Duty to Defend                                               
21      The duty to defend is broader than the duty to indemnify – “the duty to defend is 
22  triggered if the insurance policy conceivably covers the allegations in the complaint, whereas the 
23  duty to indemnify exists only if the policy actually covers the insured’s liability.” Woo v. 
24  Fireman’s Fund Ins. Co., 161 Wn. 2d 43, 53 (2007). The duty to defend “arises at the time an 
25  action is first brought, and is based on the potential for liability.” Truck Ins. Exch. v. VanPort 
26  Homes, Inc., 147 Wn. 2d 751, 760 (2002). An insurer has a duty to defend “‘when a complaint 
27  against the insured, construed liberally, alleges facts which could, if proven, impose liability 
28  upon the insured within the policy’s coverage.’” Id. (quoting Unigard Ins. Co. v. Leven, 97 Wn. 
1  App. 417, 425 (1999)).3 An insurer is not relieved of its duty to defend unless the claim alleged 
2  in the complaint is “clearly not covered by the policy.” Id. (citing Kirk v. Mt. Airy Ins. Co., 134 
3  Wn. 2d 558, 561 (1998)). Moreover, if a complaint is ambiguous, a court will construe it 
4  liberally in favor of “triggering the insurer’s duty to defend.” Id. (citing R.A. Hanson Co. v. 
5  Aetna Ins. Co., 26 Wn. App. 290, 295 (1980)). In sum, “if there is any reasonable interpretation 
6  of the facts or the law that could result in coverage, the insurer must defend.” Edmonson v. 
7  Popchoi, 172 Wn. 2d 272, 282 (2011) (citation and quotation marks omitted).  
8       “[T]o determine whether the duty to defend exists, this court examines the policy’s 
9  insuring provisions to see if the complaint’s allegations are conceivably covered. If covered, this 
10  court must then determine whether an exclusion clearly and unambiguously applies to bar 
11  coverage.” Hayden v. Mut. of Enumclaw Ins. Co., 141 Wn. 2d 55, 64 (2000). The interpretation 
12  of an insurance policy is an issue of law. Schwindt v. Underwriters at Lloyd’s of London, 81 
13  Wn. App. 293, 298 (1996). Generally, courts should “interpret insurance contracts as the 
14  average insurance purchaser would understand them,” giving undefined terms their “plain, 
15  ordinary and popular meaning.” Allstate Insurance Company v. Raynor, 143 Wn. 2d 469, 476 
16  (2001) (citations and quotation marks omitted).                          
17             i.   Policy Coverage                                          
18      Here, Ms. Schlackman’s policy provides personal liability coverage for suits “brought 
19  against an ‘insured’ for damages because of ‘bodily injury’ or ‘property damage’ caused by an 
20  ‘occurrence’ to which this coverage applies.” Dkt. # 12-1 at 36. There is no dispute that Ms. 
21  Schlackman is an “insured,” nor does plaintiff raise an argument as to whether the Underlying 
22  Complaint alleges “bodily injury,” see Dkt. # 1-1 at 80, 84 (Ms. Campbell’s allegations that she

15      As an initial matter, the Court finds plaintiff’s reliance on the elements of the claims 
16  misplaced. These mens rea requirements outline what Ms. Campbell will have to prove to

19  sufficiently state a prima facie case. Instead, the relevant question for this Court is whether the 
20  Underlying Complaint alleges facts that if proven could trigger the policy’s coverage. Thus, the 
21  Court focuses its inquiry on whether the alleged facts – not the alleged causes of action – could 
22  conceivably be viewed as an occurrence.

4  Evans v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co., 26 Wn. 2d 594 (1946); Unigard Mut. Ins. Co. v. Spokane 
5  Sch. Dist. 81, 20 Wn. App. 261, 263-64 (1978); Detweiler v. J.C. Penney Cas. Ins. Co., 110 Wn. 
6  2d 99, 104-05 (1988); Cle Elum Bowl, Inc. v. N. Pac. Ins. Co., 96 Wn. App. 698, 703-05 (1999). 
7  For purposes of liability insurance, Washington courts have stated that “an accident is never 
8  present when a deliberate act is performed unless some additional unexpected, independent and 
9  unforeseen happening occurs which produces or brings about the result of injury or death. The 
10  means as well as the result must be unforeseen, involuntary, unexpected and unusual.” Safeco 
11  Ins. Co. of Am. v. Butler, 118 Wn. 2d 383, 401 (1992) (citation omitted). An act is deliberate 
12  when it is “done with awareness of the implications or consequences of the act.” Nationwide Ins. 
13  Co. v. Hayles, Inc., 136 Wn. App. 531, 538 (2007). “All that is required is that the claimant 
14  know or should know facts from which a prudent person would conclude that the injurious 
15  consequences are reasonably foreseeable.” Lloyd v. First Farwest Life Ins. Co., 54 Wn. App. 
16  299, 302 (1989). This inquiry involves an objective, not a subjective, determination. United 
17  Servs. Auto. Ass’n v. Speed, 179 Wn. App. 184, 198 (2014) (citing Roller v. Stonewall Ins. Co., 
18  115 Wn. 2d 679, 685 (1990)). In sum, “[i]ntentional, wrongful acts will not qualify as accidents 
19  or ‘occurrences’ if the results could have been expected from the acts.” Hayles, 136 Wn. App. at 
20  538 (citing E–Z Loader Boat Trailers, Inc. v. Travelers Indem. Co., 106 Wn. 2d 901, 906 
21  (1986)).
